works.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) pollute environments worldwide, and they are toxic to many aquatic and marine animals. Yet, plastics pollution originates on land, so terrestrial animals may be particularly vulnerable to MPs. This study investigates the developmental plasticity of a terrestrial insect (variable field cricket, Gryllus lineaticeps) in response to three levels of nylon MP filaments within their diet. From hatchling stage to adulthood, crickets were fed a diet with no added MPs (control), 0.6% w/w MPs added (low), or 1.2% MPs w/w added (high). Several fitness-related traits were then measured at adulthood: survival, developmental rate, body mass and size, investment into reproductive and somatic tissues, and flight capacity. This study provides insight into the potential effects of MP exposure in an insect to assess the impact of MP pollution in terrestrial ecosystems.
works.title: From Survival to Reproduction– Developmental Plasticity to Microplastics in a Field Cricket

works.abstract: Global plastic production has been increasing exponentially, making microplastics (MPs; plastic particles < 5 mm) ubiquitous in Earth’s ecosystems, even reaching the most isolated environments and human tissues. The presence of MPs are troublesome due to their potential to cause variable levels of tissue damage and reduced reproductive ability across a range of animal taxa. Additionally, multiple factors, including biological sex, might influence the variable toxicity and sensitivity to MPs because males and females may vary in their exposure and sensitivity to MPs. In addition to their toxicity to animals, MPs release harmful phthalate esters (PAEs), which are plasticizers that give plastics their unique characteristics of flexibility and durability. Unfortunately, PAEs are also problematic to animal health because they act as endocrine disruptors and interfere with steroid hormone regulation. Yet, we lack a comprehensive understanding of the combined effects of MPs and PAEs, which may entail additive or synergistic costs to crucial traits, such as reproduction and offspring fitness. Since environments exhibit long-term contamination by MPs and PAEs, it is also essential to characterize their transgenerational effects– that is, how parental exposure to MPs and/or PAEs have carryover effects that influence their offspring who have never been exposed to these pollutants directly. Here, we used a factorial experimental design and fed four different diets (control [no additives], MPs added, PAEs added, and both MPs + PAEs added) to breeding pairs of the variable field cricket (Gryllus lineaticeps). We then determined within-generation effects on reproduction (mating success and egg production) and across-generation effects on offspring (hatching success, hatchling starvation resistance, and hatchling development rate). Our study will be the first to test for the sex-specific effects of MPs and PAEs on fitness-related traits within and across generations.
works.title: How Does Parental Exposure to Plastics Affect Offspring?

works.abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are small-sized (< 5 mm) bits of plastic present in all types of environments, including terrestrial ecosystems that are rapidly warming. Yet, the biological interplay between MPs and temperature is poorly understood in terrestrial animals. Here, we addressed three hypotheses to determine how: (1) temperature influences biological responses to MPs, (2) MPs influence thermal biology, and (3) temperature and MPs combine to influence the acquisition and allocation of resources. Specifically, we fed field crickets (Gryllus lineaticeps) different concentrations of nylon (polyamide) microfilaments while they were maintained at 23 °C, 28 °C, or 33 °C. Despite ingesting 2.5-fold more MPs, warmer individuals did not absorb more MPs into their bodies. Exposure to MPs increased investment into somatic tissue and self-maintenance, but individuals consuming MPs still had lower desiccation tolerance. Warming and MPs both promoted food consumption, but they differentially affected the life-history tradeoff between investment into self-maintenance vs. reproduction. In sum, appetite, life-history strategy, and dynamics in the digestive tract may be critical to animals simultaneously exposed to warming and MPs.
works.title: Integrating microplastics into thermal biology in an insect

works.abstract: Global plastic production is increasing exponentially, making microplastics (MPs; plastic particles <5 mm) ubiquitous in animals' environments. Microplastics can exhibit sex-specific toxicity and release harmful phthalate esters (PAEs), which are known endocrine disruptors in vertebrates and are often added to plastics to enhance flexibility and durability. Yet, we lack a comprehensive understanding of the combined biological effects of MPs and PAEs. Because environments exhibit long-term contamination by MPs and PAEs, maternal and paternal exposure to these contaminants may have carryover (transgenerational) effects on offspring. Here, we used a factorial design with dietary MPs and PAEs in the variable field cricket (Gryllus lineaticeps) to determine within-generation effects on reproduction (mating success and egg production) and across-generation effects on offspring (e.g., hatching success and hatchling developmental rates). Exposure to PAEs during early adulthood entailed significant within- and across-generational costs, including reduced parental mating success and reduced offspring hatching success, respectively. Adults exposed to PAEs also had offspring with altered developmental life histories characterized by a shortened embryonic stage and a prolonged post-embryonic stage. In contrast, the within- and across-generational effects of maternal and paternal MPs exposure were context-dependent and only evident through certain interactions. For example, MPs and PAEs interacted in a context-dependent antagonistic dynamic where exposure to one of these factors improved egg-laying, whereas exposure to both factors eliminated the observed benefit. In sum, we show that plastic pollution- particularly, PAEs- pose comprehensive threats to animals spanning from generation to generation.
works.title: Multigenerational effects of microplastics and phthalates on fitness-related traits in a field cricket

works.abstract: Contemporary fiction is shot through with the catastrophic, the dystopian, and the postapocalyptic. If we manage to take them seriously—and we should—these storyworlds of destitution and raw, oppressive survival not only reflect a dissatisfaction with the contemporary social arrangement but also a warning of what our world is careening toward: fascism, state-controlled resources, economic collapse.1 This abiding disquietude extends even to utopia, the brighter brethren of a nightmare world. As Lyman Tower Sargent reminds us, utopia “rightly upsets people because it constantly suggests that the life we lead, the society we have, is inadequate, incomplete, sick.”2 Our society is sick—and this includes its social arrangements, logistical methods, ideas and ideologies, foundational premises, repeated practices, administrative means, and forms of governance. All of these are ailing and unwell, ill and despondent of convalescence.I desire that our dystopian contemporary conditions, those which resemble and are reflected in the postapocalyptic imagination, be more urgently foregrounded for what they are: representations of the present. The present is already in crisis, already suffering the conditions of catastrophe. To put it another way, I already live in a world where people die for lack of resources, even in opulent places; where the powerful hold sway over real estate and hoard wealth and materials, forcing the less powerful into positions where they aspire to small plots of land or areas of space and expend their life’s labor toward this end; and where people are encouraged to differentiate their identities and sense of worth in comparison to others and with the assistance of controlling, hierarchical structures.I don’t want to live here.Nevertheless, the popular mediascape continually imagines such spaces for our entertainment, drawing out and sometimes intensifying contemporary realities to concentrate our attention on the projected future of our current trajectory. George Miller’s cinematic wasteland—the well-known Mad Max worldscape—presents a rich example of this practice, which exposes many unnerving aspects of our own behavior, the undergirding reality of our social systems, and our attitude toward and acceptance of dubious forms of governance. In this call for greater recognition of our present conditions in postapocalyptic narratives, I focus on the social arrangements established in the wasteland which supply the central context for the two most recent installments in the film franchise, Mad Max: Fury Road (2015) and Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga (2024), specifically to examine the control of two essential aspects of life: resources and identity.We see not only the unequal distribution of and access to resources, a tradition that began with colonization but also the ideological underpinnings of the dominant class’s control of those resources. There is no denying the intensity of income inequality and the unbalanced distribution of wealth both nationally (within the United States) and globally: this extends below monetary wealth (a marker of resource access) and into Abraham Maslow’s well-known hierarchy where poverty, destitution, and basic needs are a challenge to meet for many, if not most, of the population. Resource inequality is only maintainable by geographical domination, where the physical land—in particular the valuable centers of and access points to resources—must be cordoned off and controlled: an activity that requires force and organization. This sovereignty over space, what we call real estate in contemporary market terms, determines who comes to be situated where, which will obviously shape how they see their situation and experience their own (dis)comfort.One thing we should readily recognize is that we, the vast supermajority of us, already live largely in unintentional communities3; that is, in places we didn’t necessarily intend to be or select for ourselves to inhabit, given different options or placed under ideal circumstances, we would situate ourselves and our surrounding conditions differently. Our selection of location, of housing, and of community are restricted by and dependent upon a host of sociohistorical factors. Birth, in a general way, is foremost among these, but this also ties directly to income and class, geography, race, nation, and national, political, and cultural attitudes toward diversity and acceptance, how various in-crowds and out-crowds are determined in various contexts, and so on and so on.I already live, restricted by multiple factors, in one of these unintentional communities.Something like Pierre Bourdieu’s notions of distinction and habitus help us to bear and cope with it, psychology offers repression and cognitive dissonance as another means to trudge on, and surely the kinds of moves Marx characterized as occurring with false consciousness represent another explanation of how and why a self-destructive system seems to maintain such successful persistence. Whether I want to or not, I am in a community that contributes to a kind of insane, quite unimaginative, shortsighted, and sick system of order and living. And unless you want to deny that we live in a globalized world—a denial that seems on the political rise as of late—then you do too. In the prologue to both Fury Road and Furiosa, the images and voiceovers that accompany the opening credits frame the postapocalyptic setting for the audience: we hear the announcements of various escalating emergencies, including failures of electricity and currency, marauding gangs, and wars for oil and water. In both films, the final three utterances in this sequence are women making the following statements:“The earth is sour.”“Our bones are poisoned.”“We have become half-life.”In the context of Mad Max, we know why this is: conflict and warfare, underwritten by control over resources, land, and ideology. As the Historyman of Furiosa explains in a voiceover, “there always was, is, and will be war.”4 He then lists several recognizable historical conflicts before his list grows more ambiguous: the one-, six-, and thousand-day wars, a probable allusion to the Third World War, and then the “Oil Wars, Water Wars, the Tri-Nation Nuclear War, the Battle of the Boomtowns.” Surely a barren and precariously farmable terrain, toxins seeping into our biological, bodily makeup, and the resulting diminishment of life expectancy, can be said to come from the fallout of our proverbial and widespread deployment of atomic and thermonuclear weaponry.I don’t want to live here.But we can find these even in the pre-apocalyptic contemporary: the poisoned land of settler-colonialism and extractive capitalism that damages and depletes the soil (the earth is sour); the widespread number of chemicals, such as flame retardants and pesticides, to which the body is exposed and often already host, not to mention the ubiquity of plastic pollution (our bones are poisoned); the existential and entropic fact, writ large in the second law of thermodynamics and the energy pyramid, that our lives are coming to a close along with all other, wider life (we have become half-life).I don’t want to live here either.Fury Road and Furiosa provide extremely textured and detailed depictions of environmental disaster in a postapocalyptic worldscape: one of the “design organizing ideas,” as director George Miller points out in an interview, involves everything being “made from found objects repurposed” with “nothing manufactured” and a “regressive” result in technology and rise of “neo-medieval behavior.” These stories become more directly “allegorical,” in Miller’s words, transpiring in a “much more reduced elemental world” and told in a “much more clear, less kind of chaotic fashion” than they can be in the contemporary world. This sharp delivery of incisive themes is borne out in “every single detail that we see in the film, every prop, every vehicle, every piece of costume and also all the characters.”5While Furiosa follows the abduction, tribulations, and vengeful trail of the title character, the journey develops in the wake of a geographical power struggle as the scavenging biker band Dementus attempts to supplant Immortan Joe, controller of the sedentary economy. Immortan Joe’s control of resources is established by militant dominance and coerced labor, allowing him to hold sway over the three fortresses of the wasteland containing food, mobility, and weaponry: an elevated rock formation above an aquifer outfitted with pumps, pipes, and gardens (the Citadel); an oil-moated refinery manufacturing and monopolizing gasoline (Gastown); and a sunken lead mine used to harvest ammunition (Bullet Farm). At one point in the film, after having given a promising speech affirming his ironic disdain for “big shot” leaders and encouraging Immortan Joe’s followers and subjects to serve them instead, Dementus and his biker hoards are promptly routed. In their attempted takeover, Dementus makes a series of claims: to be one of Immortan Joe’s lieutenants (and thus a logical successor), that “we are indeed in the land of opportunity,” and that “this is our destiny.” These rhetorical moves explicitly echo Western colonial and imperial language, especially an American language of manifest destiny.Since Mad Max is set in Australia, such allusions to a manifest destiny made through conquest amplify the American capitalist (global) expansionism in which economies are monopolized and controlled by a small portion of the elite (an oligarchy of sorts). When Dementus does take control of Gastown through a clever and ruthless ruse, he is able to negotiate his new position in a meeting with Immortan Joe. In this scene, audiences see more glimpses of an intricate, appalling, and recognizable trade economy already extant between the three fortresses of the wasteland and which, we can infer, form an unsettling social network. Pursuing a doubling of all supplies transferred to Gastown in exchange for gasoline in their opening salvo, Dementus’ henchmen reveal essentials of the economy as they issue their demands: mother’s milk, hydroponics, spuds, maggot mash, and roach gruel. The identities of all these dietary commodities are easy enough to infer, and while only two (hydroponic vegetables and fruit; potatoes and other tuberous roots) are particularly desirable, they indicate a more startling economy whose extraction process exploits the bodies of the underprivileged.Maggot mash is obtained through the Citadel’s exchange with the lowest rung of Immortan Joe’s society, the destitute masses living at and around the base of the Citadel. We know this because the audience sees in two scenes that there are maggot merchants living in dugout trenches beneath the Citadel, harvesting the larvae from the rotting bodies of dead or dying human beings: at one point, an injured Furiosa finds herself awakening in such a cavern, either as a possible refugee or a potential attractant, a bait, for these merchants. She takes flight. Meanwhile, mother’s milk is produced in Immortan Joe’s Citadel fortress: it is breast milk pumped from captive women, many of whom seem to have cycled through Immortan Joe’s harem in his ongoing efforts to produce a healthy male offspring.These two cases—maggot mash and mother’s milk—display a direct and practical deployment of necro- and biopolitics in Immortan Joe’s society, which, we should say here, represents a dystopia for most.I don’t want to live here.Ideology—always accompanied by some sense of meaning-making and explanatory power, no matter how debased, crazed, or absurd—helps to hold this wasteland of scarcity together. Immortan Joe’s message of social cohesion is an authoritarian and messianic one. It is a society of concentrated power, centralized decision-making, and military spirituality. Making a social ritual out of deploying his convoys from the Citadel for supplies, early in Fury Road Immortan Joe disseminates his ideological program down upon the destitute from an elevated position in the fortress. “I am your redeemer,” he declares before releasing a small flood of water, “it is by my hand that you will rise from the ashes of this world.” At this point in the film, as the water flows, we see a wide shot of the Citadel and glimpse the high rock faces lined with lush greenery as the music rings out in a mood of positive potential. Certainly, we see a leader in Immortan Joe concerned with futurity, though it will in no sense include all members of society. The deployment of redemptive rhetoric and messianic promises, however, remains an effective tool of mass communication and conformity. We are intimately familiar with this charismatic tool: a world that is broken or fallen and needs fixing, a prognostication which can only come by the hands of the divine or semi-divine, which Immortan Joe—self-labeled as a corrupted expression of the immortal everyman—clearly proclaims. Such a world requires obedience and dependence, effectuated here though Immortan Joe’s resource control. And we can recognize, at the very least, the redemptive rhetoric of (white) Western Christianity resurfacing here and being deployed yet again to support the vices of the privileged and violent. Indeed, redemption narratives and their corresponding revenge stories are powerful and moving tales. After all, it is redemption that Furiosa is after when she rescues the five remaining wives, defecting from the society of Immortan Joe and seeking to return to the Green Place of her childhood. It is redemption for her complicity: for having participated in that society, in this world, in the perpetration of violence and awfulness that has allowed her to survive.On a practical level, the futurity of the Citadel society is concentrated on the prosperity of a select few, a hierarchical in-crowd, and is obviously not spiritual in nature: promptly shutting off the water, Immortan Joe effectively incites a riot between the lowest, poorest, and most desperate class of his society, so as to have a degree of predictable and manageable antagonism, to assert dependence, and to render ultimately the available options for classification (identity) controllable. We see Immortan Joe clearly at the center and head of this society, surrounded by a circle of warlords and privileged lieutenants, who respectively manage different aspects of resource and ideological control. We see the primary mechanism that maintains this society: the War Boys, usually young, malleable, and moribund soldiers conditioned to believe in an updated version of Valhalla where their proper military sacrifice to Immortan Joe will find them located in an afterworld of abundance and honor, where, as one War Boy puts it, they look forward to walking (or riding eternal upon petroleum powered vehicles) with their leader and “McFeasting with the heroes of all time.”6 We see internal to the War Boys is an entire hierarchical rank structure, reminiscent of militaries and infused with a mysticism that involves self-mutilation, the veneration of the combustion engines, and again, the aspiration to die in belligerent service to a higher cause: the Immortan Joe who is allegedly working to redeem the world and who holds access to the afterlife. There are other divisions of people: the useful and skilled workers (mechanics, for instance) and the possibility that promotion—social mobility—within or between some of these specialized classes can take place. There are the unskilled workers who move like rats on giant gears and rotate massive lifts. There are, as we have already mentioned, the greatest masses of the destitute beneath the Citadel, the pool of potential from which few will be drawn. And even then, they will be exploited for their utility.I don’t want to live here.In contemporary America, beholding a duplicitous leader, a politician who appropriates the vestiges of some spiritual program or promises a change, a return to the prosperous past in a coming and better future—this is commonplace and unfortunately diachronically stable. We recognize this throughout the American past. And of course, beyond America, across the globe we recognize it all over. Personality cults, even in democracies, serve their powerful function and allow the projection of our weaknesses and aspirations, our dreams and nightmares, to take their sometimes dreadful and sometimes hopeful forms. Promises of abundance persist. Their failure to be fulfilled persists. And we see, even in such drastic times as our own, declarations of hope and optimism, which slide into opportunities for complicity and persistent participation in a system whose stranglehold minimizes your potential and capacity for meaning, your options for resistance and change, and focuses your efforts (at least if that is available to on over and often of with various forms of your don’t want to live here want to do the of and complicity for all of us, both as audience members and as of an unintentional who do you see as while you these position do you you A of are you a in some for a better world, with or and you an who can help the of or a (or who the and of the A leader or for you are a or a a a or another of the destitute and on the of a in the Mad Max is not or We should not a of not my world. works.abstract: Los microplásticos son partículas de plástico que miden de 1 a 5 mm, se pueden encontrar en la arena de las playas y en otros lugares de la naturaleza y plantean graves problemas medioambientales y de salud. Como marco metodológico se aplicó el EPA’s Microplastic Beach Protocol para recolección y análisis de muestras de arena con el fin de determinar la presencia de microplásticos en el sector malecón de Playas Villamil, en la provincia del Guayas, Ecuador. Se presentan los resultados de tres muestreos realizados en noviembre de 2021, mayo y agosto de 2022. Se identificaron cinco tipos de microplásticos que son: Fragmentos, pellets, microfibras, películas plásticas y espumas. De los tres muestreos, en noviembre de 2021 se detectó la mayor cantidad de microplásticos y se registraron menores cantidades en mayo y agosto de 2022, respectivamente. La investigación sugiere una influencia estacional en la distribución y acumulación de microplásticos. Los hallazgos plantean la necesidad de ampliar el alcance geográfico y la frecuencia de los estudios para comprender mejor la magnitud del problema y desarrollar estrategias efectivas de prevención y mitigación. Se subraya la importancia de adoptar medidas preventivas y correctivas para abordar esta problemática global.
works.journal: Acta Oceanografica del Pacifico/Acta Oceanográfica del Pacífico
works.title: Identificación y Análisis de Microplásticos en la Zona Costera de Playas (General Villamil), provincia del Guayas, Ecuador

works.abstract: Underwater marine debris poses significant threats to marine ecosystems and coastal environments, yet remains largely invisible to traditional satellite-based monitoring systems. We present Neural Oceans, a forecasting system for predicting underwater debris accumulation patterns using physics-informed deep learning. Our two-phase methodology combines Lagrangian particle simulation driven by real oceanographic data with a convolutional neural network - long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) architecture for spatiotemporal prediction. We generate training data through a realistic particle transport simulation incorporating 157,550 underwater debris particles released at SeaClear H2020 survey sites across the Mediterranean Sea. Our physics-informed feature engineering creates 17 hydrodynamic variables capturing multi-scale transport processes. The CNN-LSTM model processes 7-day environmental sequences to predict debris density fields 36 hours ahead with uncertainty quantification. Evaluation on 172 training sequences demonstrates an R2value equal to 0.623, a correlation of 0.791, and a hotspot F1-score equal to 0.710. The 72 × 325 spatial resolution enables regional marine management applications while remaining computationally tractable for real-time deployment. Neural Oceans addresses critical gaps in marine debris monitoring by providing forecasting capability with practical lead times for cleanup prioritization, survey optimization, and marine protected area management.
works.journal: International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications
works.title: Neural Oceans: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Underwater Marine Debris Forecasting

works.abstract: Environmental context Microplastics are a new source of toxic compounds in marine and freshwater environments. This research documents the discovery of microplastic fibres in the seawater column and the chemical analysis of associated toxic chemicals in microplastic marine debris. Microplastic pollution is pervasive and hazardous. Abstract Initial studies of floating plastic debris in the oceans dealt with macroscopic particles. This research found microscale plastic present as well. Chemical analysis of sorbed materials revealed toxic materials associated with the microparticles. Seawater and plastic fragment samples were collected in September 2007 in the North Pacific Central Gyre. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) were detected by mass spectrometry in extracts from the plastic fragments. Net concentrations of PCBs ranged from 1 to 223 ng g–1 plastic. The most common synthetic polymers were found to be polypropylene and polyethylene. Microscopic plastic fibres and particles were also discovered in the seawater samples and examined by scanning electron microscopy. Analysis of filtered seawater samples also revealed toxic materials in concentrations lower than found on the plastic particles.
works.title: Characterisation of microplastics and toxic chemicals extracted from microplastic samples from the North Pacific Gyre

works.abstract: Floating marine plastic debris was found to function as solid-phase extraction media, adsorbing and concentrating pollutants out of the water column. Plastic debris was collected in the North Pacific Gyre, extracted, and analyzed for 36 individual PCB congeners, 17 organochlorine pesticides, and 16 EPA priority PAHs. Over 50% contained PCBs, 40% contained pesticides, and nearly 80% contained PAHs. The PAHs included 2, 3 and 4 ring congeners. The PCBs were primarily CB-11, 28, 44, 52, 66, and 101. The pesticides detected were primarily p,p-DDTs and its metabolite, o,p-DDD, as well as BHC (a,b,g and d). The concentrations of pollutants found ranged from a few ppb to thousands of ppb. The types of PCBs and PAHs found were similar to those found in marine sediments. However, these plastic particles were mostly polyethylene which is resistant to degradation and although functioning similarly to sediments in accumulating pollutants, these had remained on or near the ocean surface. Particles collected included intact plastic items as well as many pieces less than 5 mm in size.
works.title: Quantitation of persistent organic pollutants adsorbed on plastic debris from the Northern Pacific Gyre's “eastern garbage patch”
Persistent organic pollutants carried by synthetic polymers in the ocean environment

works.abstract: Synthetic polymers are extremely useful for a wide variety of applications. Although there are many types and combinations of polymers, they typically share the property of being relatively resistant to biodegradation and they are cheap. This means they are widely used and discarded. An amazing amount finds its way into the oceans. Charles Moore (2001) found, far at sea in the Pacific, some six times by mass more plastic material in the ocean than zooplankton. These plastic materials are ingested by marine life. Moore has also collected samples of plastic parts from the bodies of sea birds that died with large amounts of plastic materials in them. Another research group, Mato (2001) has reported that the starting materials, polypropylene plastic pellets, used for fabrication by injection molding can be shown to concentrate polychlorinated biphenyls, PCBs, dichlorodiphenyldichloroethylene, DDE, and nonylphenol, NP. We are developing the analytical methods to extract, concentrate and identify persistent organic pollutants (POPs) that may have accumulated in plastic particles in the ocean. Cap.Charles Moore (AMRF) has provided samples collected in the North Pacific for our analysis.
works.title: Pollution Carried by Synthetic Polymers in the Ocean
